fields.title: Significance Threshold
fields.keyTakeaway: Optimization is justified when it changes the perception category, yields a measurable behavioral effect, reduces costs, or prevents a growing problem—and is unjustified in other cases.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: The team proposes speeding up a screen from 700 to 500 milliseconds. Is it worth it?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Optimization is attractive work with a measurable result, and it easily consumes time that should go into the product. At the same time, skipping necessary optimization is also expensive. An explicit criterion is needed.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Three questions before a performance task.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Does the improvement change the perception category?** According to the table from `PF1-N2-L2`: 700 → 500 ms stays within "fast", a person won't notice. 4 s → 2 s moves it from "annoyance" to "waiting"—they will notice.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Is there a behavioral effect?** Drop-off data depending on time answers this directly. If drop-off does not differ between 500 and 700 ms, the improvement won't pay off.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **What is the component's share and maximum gain?** Amdahl's law from `PF2-N2-L1`.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: [[significance-threshold|Significance threshold]] for consumer products usually runs at 20% relative improvement or crossing a category boundary. Anything less does not justify weeks of work.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: When to optimize regardless of these rules:
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: *Growing problem.* Currently 800 ms, with 3x growth it will become 2.5 s. Fixing it is cheaper now. *Cost.* An improvement that reduces infrastructure costs pays off in money, not perception. *Unblocking.* A slow component prevents building a feature.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: And the [[premature-optimization|inverse rule]]: optimizing something that doesn't yet work under load is almost always premature. First measure, then improve.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Declined:* speeding up product card from 480 to 320 ms. Within the "fast" category, drop-off doesn't differ, component share 11%. Two weeks of work for an imperceptible improvement.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *Approved:* reducing the main screen response size. Not about speed, but traffic: 42 TB a month at 5.7 RUB/GB. A 30% reduction is 820k saved per year for a week of work.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *Approved:* speeding up the order history screen from 2.9 to 1.1 s. No one complained, but the screen crossed a category boundary, and with database growth would become even slower—N+1 scales with the number of orders.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: The last case is an example of the "growing problem" rule: imperceptible now, an outage in a year.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: The criterion does not apply to scenarios where speed is part of the product's value. For search or a trading terminal, 200 ms versus 400 is a fundamental difference, even though both are within "fast".
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Optimization is justified when it changes the perception category, yields a measurable behavioral effect, reduces costs, or prevents a growing problem—and is unjustified in other cases.
